content: 1. Rabies Incubation and Epidemiology: Studies have demonstrated that human rabies can have a prolonged incubation period lasting several years. This highlights the importance of understanding the disease's natural history and its epidemiological patterns to improve prevention and control strategies. 2. Global Rabies Control Efforts: Rabies transmitted by dogs has been successfully eliminated in regions such as North America, Western Europe, Japan, and parts of Asia and South America. However, it remains endemic in over 100 countries, primarily in the developing world. Controlling rabies in dogs is critical to preventing human cases, as dogs are responsible for over 95% of human rabies transmissions. 3. Dog Vaccination Campaigns: Mass vaccination of dogs is the cornerstone of rabies control programs. To achieve herd immunity and prevent the spread of the virus, at least 70% of the dog population must be vaccinated annually. Campaigns should be well-planned, recurrent, and adapted to local dog population dynamics, including free-roaming and community-owned dogs. 4. Vaccination Strategies: Various approaches can be used to vaccinate dogs, including house-to-house visits, fixed vaccination posts, mobile teams, and temporary vaccination sites. The choice of method should consider the local sociocultural context and aim to maximize coverage. 5. Inclusion of Puppies in Vaccination: Puppies, including those under three months of age, should be vaccinated during campaigns, as studies have shown they can mount an effective immune response with high-quality vaccines. 6. Monitoring and Identification: Vaccinated dogs should be identified using temporary or permanent markers, such as collars or tags, to monitor vaccination coverage and differentiate unvaccinated animals. This is essential for evaluating the success of campaigns and planning follow-up activities. 7. Community Engagement and Education: Educational campaigns can improve participation in vaccination programs and enhance their sustainability. 8. Cost-Effectiveness of Dog Vaccination: Free vaccination campaigns are generally more effective in achieving high coverage compared to fee-based programs, which may reduce participation. 9. Vaccine Quality and Cold Chain Maintenance: Rabies vaccines must meet international standards for potency, safety, and efficacy. Maintaining the cold chain (2–8°C) is critical to preserving vaccine effectiveness. Vaccines inducing immunity for at least two years are recommended for annual campaigns. 10. Strategic Planning and Intersectoral Cooperation: Rabies control programs require a One Health approach, involving collaboration between veterinary services, public health authorities, and wildlife management. 11. Surveillance and Diagnostics: Strengthening diagnostic capacity and surveillance systems is essential for timely detection and reporting of rabies cases. Rapid diagnostic tests and cross-border collaboration can further enhance control efforts. 12. Elimination Goals: Rabies elimination requires sustained efforts, including mass dog vaccination, public education, and access to PEP. 13. Challenges in Dog Population Management: Free-roaming dogs play a significant role in rabies transmission and must be included in vaccination campaigns. Dog removal strategies are ineffective and may undermine vaccination efforts, particularly in areas with high dog population turnover. 14. Research and Innovation: Continued research is needed to improve vaccination methods, identify cost-effective dog identification techniques, and develop vaccines with longer-lasting immunity. These advancements will support global efforts to eliminate rabies. 15. International Standards and Guidelines: Rabies vaccines for animals should comply with national and international standards. In the absence of adequate national regulations, reference should be made to guidelines from organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE). By implementing these strategies, rabies control programs can effectively reduce the burden of the disease and move closer to the goal of global elimination.
